Hong Leong Holdings-TID joint venture submits top bid of $1,755 psf ppr for Orchard Boulevard GLS site
article:
The tender for a Government Land Sale (GLS) site at Orchard Boulevard closed on Oct 29, drawing five bids. A joint venture between Hong Leong Holdings and TID submitted the top bid of $181.86 million, or $1,755 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), for the residential plot that can yield about 110 units.

Bids received for the Orchard Boulevard GLS site

The joint venture’s bid is 8.3% above the next-highest offer of $167.85 million ($1,620 psf ppr), submitted by Global Resource Construction, the Singapore-listed construction arm of property developer SingHaiyi Group .

The lowest bid, from a consortium led by Macly Group and Roxy-Pacific Holdings, was $139.9 million ($1,350 psf ppr). That is 30% lower than the top offer.

The bids received for the Orchard Boulevard site were within analysts’ expectations of four to five offers with a top bid of $1,650 to $2,050 psf ppr.

The highest bid is also 8.5% more than the $1,617 psf ppr UOL Group and Singapore Land Group (SingLand) paid in 2024 for a nearby plot that is now the site of the 301-unit UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard . The developers beat three other bidders for the site.

Wong Siew Yieng, head of research and content at PropNex, sees the top bid for the latest Orchard Boulevard site as "a firm one". "It is the third highest land rate for a pure residential GLS plot in the CCR since 2018, after the Peck Hay Road site which was awarded for $1,865 psf ppr in June 2026 and the Bukit Timah Road plot that fetched $1,820 psf ppr in November 2025," she says.

The wide spread in bid prices suggest developers had differing assessments of the site and upcoming supply in the CCR. "Developers are likely to have weighed the several prime GLS sites sold since November 2025 that have yet to be launched," Wong notes. Comprising plots at Bukit Timah Road, Dunearn Road, Holland Plain, Peck Hay Road and River Valley Green (Parcel C), the sites could potentially offer around 1,700 new homes in the region.

Compared to the UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard plot, the "more manageable" development scale of the latest Orchard Boulevard GSL site may have contributed to developer participation, says Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI.

Developers were also likely motivated by UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard's performance. Launched for sale in July 2025, the  luxury residential project moved 162 units (53.8%) on its launch day at an average price of $3,350 psf. Caveats lodged as of Oct 28 show that the project is now 82.7% taken up, with prices averaging $3,405 psf.

"The strong take up at UpperHouse suggests that there remains a pool of buyers willing to commit to new homes in the area, supported by the site's prime location, connectivity and proximity to the Orchard Road shopping and lifestyle belt," Sandrasegeran says.

Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, adds that UpperHouse at Orchard Boulevard saw a median selling price of $3,668 psf in 3Q2026, which provides "key pricing support" for future projects in the area.

Prime location close to Orchard Road shopping belt

The Orchard Boulevard site measures 37,006 sq ft and has a maximum gross floor area of 103,624 sq ft.

Located at the corner of Orchard Road and Tomlinson Road, the 99-year leasehold plot is surrounded by luxury residential developments such as the 150-unit Cuscaden Residences on Cuscaden Road, the 54-unit Park Nova on Tomlinson Road and the 154-unit Boulevard 88 on Orchard Boulevard.

It is also within walking distance of the Orchard Boulevard MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line — one stop away from the Orchard Road MRT Station, which is an interchange with the North-South line.

"Developers would have been drawn by the site's direct proximity to Orchard Road, Orchard Boulevard MRT station and the sales performance of nearby new recent launches, which provide tangible benchmarks for pricing and absorption," comments Leonard Tay, Knight Frank Singapore's head of reserve.

Basd on the top bid of $1,755 psf ppr, he estimates the future development could launch with average selling prices "in the region of $3,600 psf".

Meanwhile, Tricia Song, CBRE's head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia, projects launch prices to average around $3,450 to $3,550 psf.

title: StarHub vs Singtel: Which Singapore Telco Is the Better Dividend Stock?
article:
Telco shares are not meant to be exciting.
You can even call it boring.
People pay their phone bills every month, the telco earns a profit, and the dividends should arrive like clockwork.
But is that true for both
StarHub Ltd
(SGX: CC3) and
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel?
The duo offer mobile services to Singapore investors.
Both face price wars, rising costs, and heavy network spending.
If that’s the case: which one makes the better
dividend stock
?
For that, we have to dive into the latest financials to see which company has better dividend sustainability and potential long-term capital returns.
StarHub vs Singtel: Two Different Business Models
StarHub primarily serves the Singapore market.
It sells mobile, broadband and pay-TV plans, and also offers companies services like managed IT and cybersecurity.
Consumer plans, which mostly run on monthly bills, brought in about 61% of its service revenue in the six months to 30 June 2026 (1H2026), excluding Ensign.
But average revenue per user is falling, with mobile service revenue down 10.5% year on year and broadband down 8.7% over the same period.
StarHub is targeting S$70 million in yearly cost savings by 2028, with about 10% completed thus far.
Enterprise, the other 39%, is the growth plan.
StarHub’s orderbook is up about 52% year on year (YoY), yet regional enterprise revenue slipped 1.8% to S$290.8 million.
Cybersecurity is a priority, though StarHub — to our knowledge — hasn’t provided any breakdown of its contribution.
Staying Singapore-only is a double-edged sword.
On the upside, it enables StarHub to establish a strong position in a compact market with no currency risk.
But there is nowhere to hide when there is a consumer price war.
In contrast, Singtel is a
diversified
business.
Singtel owns Singtel Singapore and Optus in Australia, plus stakes in associate telcos such as Bharti Airtel in India, AIS in Thailand, and Globe in the Philippines.
Those associates earned S$543 million in the first quarter ending 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027).
The telco’s growth engines these days are data centres alongside enterprise services under Digital InfraCo and NCS, respectively.
When Singapore weakens, Optus and the regional associates can help soften the blow.
Related articles:
Singtel vs StarHub: Examining Free Cash Flow Payout Ratios for Income Investors
Earnings Review: How 4 Singapore Stocks Are Navigating Global and Local Headwinds
Which Telco Has the Stronger Financial Performance?
At first glance, StarHub’s 1H2026 profit of S$258.1 million looks great.
It isn’t.
Most of it is a one-off gain from ending an arrangement with Ensign, which is now an associate.
Without the gain, profit was S$12.4 million.
StarHub expects 2026 EBITDA of just 75% to 80% of last year’s S$403.6 million.
Singtel’s profit is cleaner.
In 1QFY2027, Singtel’s underlying profit rose 21% to S$831 million.
Without a one-off gain, underlying profit still grew 15%.
EBITDA climbed 9% to S$1.08 billion.
Singtel reports cash flow and debt only twice a year, so the latest figures available are for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026).
It generated S$2.44 billion of
free cash flow
(FCF) in FY2026.
StarHub’s 2025 FCF was negative S$24 million.
Excluding a S$188 million spectrum payment made during that year, FCF would have been S$163.3 million.
In 1H2026, FCF came in at S$40.6 million.
On debt, Singtel’s net debt at the end of FY2026 came in at S$8.7 billion with an interest cover of 19 times.
StarHub’s debt as of 30 June 2026 was S$847.4 million with a net debt to EBITDA of 2.39 times.

StarHub’s policy is to pay at least 80% of adjusted profit, but for 2026 it promised at least S$0.06 a share.
That is about S$110 million a year.
Singtel pays two dividends.
The core dividend is 60.9% of LTM underlying profit but 125% of FCF.
The other is the value realisation dividend (VRD), expected to be between S$0.03 and S$0.06 per share per year, paid from asset sales.
FY2026 had S$0.051.
Together they cost S$3.0 billion in cash, against FCF of S$2.44 billion.
Asset sales filled the gap.
Singtel has recycled about S$6.8 billion since April 2024, roughly 75% of its S$9 billion target, and expects S$0.7 billion in special dividends from AIS and Gulf in FY2027.
In this case, the higher yield is more sustainable: StarHub’s 5.6% is well covered by cash and earnings.
What Could Drive Future Growth?
StarHub needs cost cuts and enterprise orders to lift margins, then turn them into cash.
Capital expenditure (Capex) of 13% to 15% of revenue will absorb some of it.
Singtel’s growth is more varied.
It expects operating profit to rise in the low-to-mid single digits in FY2027, and Digital InfraCo revenue grew 19% in 1QFY2027.
Elsewhere, Singel bought data centre operator STT GDC and plans a GPU cluster costing up to S$600 million.
A buyback of roughly S$1+ billion outstanding adds to returns.

StarHub looks cheaper on earnings and FCF yield.
On the other hand, Singtel’s 20.7x is richer, though profit is growing and you also get broader geographical exposure.
The market is pricing in stronger growth for Singtel, while StarHub is priced cheaper for operational recovery.
What Are the Biggest Risks for Dividend Investors?
Price competition comes first, as cheaper plans shrink what each customer pays.
Networks also never stop costing money, and higher borrowing costs would eat into dividends.
Then comes the company risks.
StarHub depends on Singapore alone and must deliver its transformation.
Singtel faces overseas operating risks, currency swings and reliance on associates.
Get Smart: Which Telco Would I Buy for Dividends?
Overall, StarHub seems the better dividend buy.
StarHub has the higher yield at 5.6%, which is covered by earnings and cash flows.
Singtel’s 4.5% is lower, yet its core dividend (3.2%) is covered by earnings, cash generation and asset recycling.
It also has the stronger balance sheet and a growing payout, up 9% YoY to S$0.185.
The extra dividend leans on asset sales, so it could shrink.
StarHub could win this call if EBITDA stabilises and the group returns to growth.

title: Google shares drop after 3Q sales miss reignites fears over AI
article:
(Oct 29): Alphabet Inc’s shares fell about 10% in early trading, setting the stock up for its biggest-ever market value wipeout, after the company reported disappointing search and advertising sales that reinforced investor concerns about artificial intelligence’s (AI) threat to its core business.

 

The Google parent reported sales, excluding partner payouts, of US$111.2 billion for the third quarter (3Q), falling short of analysts’ projections. Ad sales from search and other channels — a business line that accounts for roughly half of overall revenue and is critical to financing the massive AI investments — also missed forecasts, growing at the slowest pace in five quarters. 

 

The results and share reaction “show us the margin for error when a hyperscaler spending hundreds of billions on the AI infrastructure buildout” posts disappointing results in its core business, JPMorgan analysts including Doug Anmuth said in a note.

If Alphabet’s premarket share decline holds, it will cut more than US$395 billion from Alphabet’s market value. The shares closed at US$324.89 in New York on Wednesday and have gained 3.8% this year. The company’s performance stood in particularly stark contrast to rival Microsoft Corp, which reported growth in its cloud business that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations while keeping its spending in check, stoking a rally in its stock.

Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said in an earnings call with investors late on Wednesday that the growing popularity of AI Mode, a new tab in Google Search, took a toll on the company’s results. AI queries have “lower monetisation,” Schindler said, though he noted that the company was optimistic and has plans to bring more ads to that part of the search engine.

For years, Google executives have argued that AI chatbots and features won’t cut significantly into its search business. But investors have worried about the impact on the company’s cash cow as consumers turn to rival to ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s own AI features.

The pressure is mounting on Alphabet chief executive officer Sundar Pichai to justify the more than US$1 trillion that Google is facing in future payments on resources such as data centres, computing and energy to power his AI ambitions. “This quarter feels like a moment of truth for Alphabet: Either Pichai and his team fix the way the company monetises AI, or the giant risks losing its leadership in several of its core businesses in the near future,” said Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com.

See also: Alphabet’s revenue miss reignites fears over AI spending binge

“Until Google shows it can charge for AI the way it once charged for search ads,” he said, every capital spending forecast it issues is going to “read less like ambition and more like a bill”.

Google’s sprint to build AI infrastructure for both itself and customers has sent the firm’s capital expenditures soaring to record levels. The firm is working to overhaul popular products such as the search engine, YouTube and Gmail with AI. But those efforts have yet to yield the kind of revenue the investors want to see to justify all the spending.

Google’s overall services revenue totalled US$96.3 billion in 3Q, below estimates for US$98.4 billion. YouTube advertising sales of US$11.2 billion also fell below projections.

See also: Memory stocks lost their shine despite strong earnings

In the meantime, Google’s AI bets are getting even more expensive. By the end of 3Q, Google’s future commitments to buy resources such as computing power and energy totaled US$924 billion. Upcoming obligations such as data-centre leases that haven’t yet commenced hit US$152 billion, bringing the company’s total future obligations to well over US$1 trillion.

For the second quarter in a row, the company posted negative free cash flow, something it had, up until now, never seen since going public.

“Search still generates the bulk of Alphabet’s cash, and two straight quarters of negative free cash flow show the pure AI math isn’t working right now,” said Anders Bylund, contributing tech analyst at the Motley Fool.

Alphabet said in July that capital expenditures will reach as much as US$205 billion this year, more than double what it spent last year. AI requires massive amounts of computing power, and Google is racing to build data centres so it can meet demand for AI from consumers, businesses and its own employees.

Alphabet’s equity investments also weighed on the company’s bottom line. Those stakes posted an US$8.7 billion loss, in large part due to Alphabet’s SpaceX position. That’s a sharp reversal from the gains it saw a year earlier and the windfall in the second quarter that was mainly driven by SpaceX and an investment in a private company that Bloomberg later identified as Anthropic PBC.

Its 3Q net income was US$2.12 a share, falling far below Wall Street’s estimate of US$2.99.

One bright spot in the report was Google Cloud, which is seen as a key gauge of demand for the company’s AI products and hosting services. The division reported sales of US$30.7 billion and profit of US$11.1 billion, surpassing analyst estimates of US$29.1 billion in revenue and US$9.8 billion in profit. Among the unit’s biggest customers are startups such as Anthropic that compete with Google in the AI race.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“Cloud is booming, but many of its best customers are building assistants that are already beating Google with consumers,” Monteiro wrote. “Right now, Alphabet earns more selling AI to its rivals than using it itself, and that gap should keep growing over the next few quarters unless its models change drastically, and quickly.”

Over the past few years, Google has been working to reinvent its search engine for the AI age, trying to keep consumers in the habit of relying on its answers even as chatbots from OpenAI and Anthropic become more popular. The company now delivers AI-generated answers in response to many searches, a shift that has had major implications for businesses that have traditionally relied on the search giant for traffic and advertising revenue.

Google has worked particularly hard on building an edge by generating more personalised responses to questions, leveraging years of information about its users. In recent months, though, the company has fallen behind Anthropic and OpenAI in developing AI coding tools. Google recently released Gemini 4, which it says excels in areas such as coding and cybersecurity, though some employees fear the company has yet to fully catch up.

Hours before its earnings call, Google announced yet another new AI model known as Carbon, a potential answer to the critics who’ve called for the company to speed up the pace of AI development.

“We have more models coming soon,” Pichai told analysts on the call, “including more efficient versions to help developers optimize for speed and cost and to deploy across our billions of users”.

title: Lagarde to leave ECB early, igniting race to replace her
article:
President Christine Lagarde announced she’ll leave the European Central Bank in early 2027, intensifying the struggle to replace one of the world’s most powerful monetary policymakers.

Lagarde will step down on Feb 7, according to an ECB statement Thursday. She became the institution’s fourth leader, and the second from France, when she replaced Mario Draghi in 2019. Her term was due to end in October 2027.

Her departure sets up one of Europe’s most consequential leadership contests, with the winner to oversee interest rates for the euro zone’s 21 member states and their more than 350 million people.

The move comes at a delicate time for the Frankfurt-based ECB, which is battling elevated inflation caused by the Iran war, against a backdrop of volatile geopolitics, nervy bond markets and massive European spending on defense and infrastructure.

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos and the Netherlands’ Klaas Knot are vying for Lagarde’s job. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October reckon De Cos, a former Bank of Spain chief who currently heads the Bank for International Settlements, is favorite.

Talk about Lagarde’s exit had been building. She’d repeatedly declined to commit to finishing her eight-year term. Speculation has been rife, meanwhile, that she wants to take over the World Economic Forum, the organizer of the annual Davos gathering.

See also: Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul

Lagarde has also indicated she may like to play a role in campaigning for French presidential elections next spring, but ruled out running for the top job. The cryptic remarks have frustrated colleagues at the ECB, with some worrying it’s a bad look for one of the region’s most important economic institutions.

The announcement arrives with the US and Iran still failing to strike a lasting peace deal. The ECB lifted borrowing costs in June and September, and markets expect policy to be tightened further.

Bond yields, meanwhile, have spiked around the globe, with investors becoming particularly nervous about public finances in Lagarde’s home country of France. The premium they demand to hold the nation’s 10-year bonds compared with those of Germany recently hit its highest since 2011, leading to speculation of possible ECB intervention.

See also: Spotify keeps adding users in 3Q but misses slightly on revenue

While Lagarde has argued that projections point to inflation returning toward target around the end of 2027, critics will accuse her of breaking promises to not abandon her post when “there are clouds on the horizon”.

Before Lagarde, the Netherlands’ Wim Duisenberg was the only president to not complete a full term. But his curtailed stint was agreed in advance to resolve a deadlock between France and Germany before the ECB’s inception in 1998.

European leaders have summits in November and December where they try to select a successor. Beyond the front-runners, an outsider can’t be excluded, with Lagarde herself having only entered the frame at the last minute.

Governments must also select a successor for Isabel Schnabel, who’s cutting her term short by a year and will leave in early 2027 to join the the International Monetary Fund. With Chief Economist Philip Lane’s mandate also up in May, they’ll probably seek to strike a deal on all three positions.

Lagarde’s premature departure risks drawing accusations of political encroachment on the ECB’s independence, as the timeline now allows President Emmanuel Macron to help replace her before his final terms ends. Polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen could win the first round of elections for the Elysee.

France’s central-bank chief also resigned early, with Macron appointing Emmanuel Moulin, his chief of staff, to the position.

title: Aztech rejects US$19.4 mil claim of damages from customer; mulls counter claim
article:
Just as Aztech Global was suffering from target price cuts by analysts, the manufacturer says a customer is alleging breach of contract and is requesting damages of some US$19.4 million to be paid by November 3.

According to Aztech, via a subsidiary, it has been providing certain development, industrialisation and manufacturing services provided to the customer, who was not named.

Aztech says the customer has also claimed that two representatives of its subsidiary, described as key decision makers, are personally liable to the customer on various grounds including, but not limited to misrepresentation, inducing breach of contract and conspiracy.

Aztech rejects these claims entirely and is denying any liability.

"The group considers the claims to be without merit and will vigorously defend them to safeguard its reputation and that of its representatives. The Group also intends to pursue its own claims against the customer and is seeking legal advice accordingly," says Aztech.

Aztech Global shares closed at 38 cents on Oct 29, down 6.17% for the day.

title: Sembcorp Industries grows Singapore power portfolio with new power plant; to explore energy solutions with DayOne
article:
Sembcorp Industries’s 600MW hydrogen-ready combined-cycle gas turbine (CCGT) power plant on Jurong Island has commenced commercial operations, according to an Oct 28 announcement.

With the new facility, Sembcorp’s total gas-fired and renewables portfolio is now 5.7GW in Singapore, with these assets supporting the growing power demand from Singapore’s data centre and semiconductor sectors. Complementing the generation capacity are more than 2GW of regional renewable energy import opportunities.

“This new capacity strengthens our ability to power Singapore’s AI-driven growth and enhance the nation’s energy resilience,” says Koh Chiap Khiong, CEO of gas and related services for Sembcorp. “Fully contracted under long-term arrangements, the plant will deliver reliable power while supporting Singapore’s longer-term energy transition.”

Separately, Sembcorp also announced that subsidiary Sembcorp Utilities has signed an MoU with DayOne Data Centers. Under the MoU, Sembcorp will serve as DayOne’s technical partner for selected data centre projects, drawing on its capabilities across the energy value chain to evaluate solutions that support their power requirements, including potential opportunities in the region.

With the proliferation of AI adoption, the energy requirements of data centres are becoming increasingly complex. Through the collaboration, Sembcorp and DayOne will explore how different energy solutions can support these projects, from onsite power infrastructure and generation to fuel supply, renewable energy generation, and operations and maintenance services.

“Powering AI will require energy solutions that can keep pace with the scale and pace of data centre growth,” says Koh, who is also CEO of Singapore, Sembcorp. “Our collaboration with DayOne allows us to work together on solutions tailored to the needs of its developments.”

See also: Seatrium and Karpowership explore JV for floating power solutions in Singapore

DayOne CEO Jamie Khoo says: “For DayOne, we think about customers’ requirements in scalable land, power, energy and other critical resources from the earliest stages of development. Partnering with Sembcorp gives us an opportunity to explore integrated data centre and energy solutions to support DayOne’s continued expansion across the region.”

title: South Korea's FuriosaAI quadruples value to US$2.9 bil in Nvidia chase
article:
(Oct 29): South Korean artificial intelligence (AI) chip start-up FuriosaAI quadrupled its valuation to US$2.9 billion ($3.7 billion) in a fresh funding round, bolstering its bid to challenge the likes of Nvidia Corp.

The Seoul-based upstart said on Thursday it raised US$620 million in a Series D round from investors including US-based Infinitum Partners. South Korea’s National Growth Fund contributed US$280 million and international investors US$110 million, with Jericho Capital, Worldline Capital, Singapore’s QUDA Capital and Abu Dhabi-based NeoFort Holding among backers.

Investors are hunting for alternatives for Nvidia chips that dominate AI data centres, seeking more energy-efficient silicon. That shift centres on inference — generating outputs from trained AI models — which is emerging as one of the industry’s primary cost battlegrounds as rising demand boosts power needs.

Founded in 2017, FuriosaAI began mass production of RNGD — pronounced “renegade” — chips in January and is working with Broadcom Inc on a third-generation accelerator targeting large-scale AI infrastructure. The start-up is betting that its chip architecture, designed to minimise energy-intensive data movement, will help it gain ground in the Nvidia-led market. Its previous round last year valued the company at US$735 million.

FuriosaAI is engaged with a large number of customers in the Asia-Pacific region and Middle East, chief executive officer June Paik said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Thursday. “We see strong demand and opportunities as we are scaling our business globally.”

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co is producing 20,000 RNGD accelerators this year, with the South Korean start-up aiming to more than double output to over 40,000 units in 2027. Samsung SDS, LG Group and South Korean AI start-up Upstage are among those that are using the chips.

See also: Nvidia-backed firm launches US$3.1 bil GPU loan in market

Existing backers Naver Corp, Korea Development Bank, DSC Investment, Nextrans and Kakao Investment also joined the financing round, while the Export-Import Bank of Korea made its first direct start-up investment in FuriosaAI.

title: Air Liquide’s sales grow on sustained AI-related demand
article:
(Oct 29): Air Liquide SA revenue grew to its highest in nearly four years, propelled by increased demand in its artificial intelligence (AI)-exposed unit.

Third-quarter revenue in the electronics business, which supplies ultra-pure specialty gases and advanced materials to semiconductor factories grew 12% on a comparable basis. Overall sales rose to €7.3 billion, ahead of the €7.1 billion analysts had expected.

Paris-listed Air Liquide is one of the three main providers of industrial gases, along with Linde Plc and Air Products and Chemicals Inc, and supplies industrial gases and advanced materials used in chipmaking.

Growth for the unit came mostly from Asia, with momentum for carrier gases driven by the start-up and ramp-up of new production units, particularly in China, the group said in a Thursday statement. Demand for some of the unit’s other products came from South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Japan.

The company said it invested over €170 million in Japan for the supply ultra-pure gases to “support market momentum in semiconductors and AI.”

Investments in the electronics business to support AI almost doubled in the first nine months of the year compared to the full year 2025, the company said.

See also: Ports giant DP World redraws Hormuz logistics with truck bet

The company also said it launched the first €1 billion tranche of its share buyback programme announced earlier this month, seeking to assuage pressure from Elliott Investment Management. It reiterated its financial guidance.
